scope: Use the Shockley square law and the transconductance relations to find drain current, gate-source voltage, g_m, r_d and voltage gain for an n-channel JFET.
intuition: A JFET is a bar of silicon with a reverse-biased gate junction wrapped around it. Increasing the reverse gate voltage widens the depletion region and squeezes the conducting channel, so the drain current falls. At V_GS(off) the channel is fully pinched shut and only a trickle flows.
concept: **Structure and why the gate draws no current.** An n-channel JFET is a lightly doped n-type channel with two heavily doped $p^{+}$ gate regions diffused into its sides; the gate and channel form a $p^{+}n$ junction that is **always reverse biased** in normal operation. Because the junction is reverse biased, the gate current is only the reverse saturation current, typically nanoamps, so the gate presents a very high input resistance (megohms to hundreds of megohms) and the device is controlled by the gate *voltage*, not by gate current. That is the fundamental break from the BJT, whose forward-biased input junction demands real base current. The gate is used only to modulate the width of the depletion region that extends into the channel.

**Two regions, and the boundary between them.** With a small $V_{DS}$ the channel behaves as a voltage-controlled resistor: increasing $V_{GS}$ (more reverse bias) raises the channel resistance. This is the **ohmic or triode region**, and it exists only while $V_{DS}$ is smaller than the pinch-off boundary $V_{DS(sat)}=V_{GS}-V_{GS(off)}=V_{GS}+V_P$. As $V_{DS}$ grows, the voltage drop along the channel makes the depletion region near the drain wider than near the source, and at $V_{DS}=V_{DS(sat)}$ the two depletion regions meet at the drain end: the channel is **pinched off**. Pinch-off is not a shutdown — the voltage across the pinched section is fixed at $V_{DS(sat)}$, so the current through it is fixed and further increases in $V_{DS}$ only widen the depletion region toward the source. The drain current therefore becomes nearly constant: this is the **saturation or constant-current region**, and it is where the JFET is used as an amplifier. The current at $V_{GS}=0$, measured well into the constant-current region, is the data-sheet parameter $I_{DSS}$; the (negative for n-channel) gate voltage that reduces the current to essentially zero is $V_{GS(off)}=-V_P$, where $V_P$ is the pinch-off voltage as a positive magnitude.

**The transfer characteristic is a square law.** The Shockley equation $I_D=I_{DSS}\left(1-\frac{|V_{GS}|}{V_P}\right)^{2}$ is a parabola on the transfer curve, controlled at three points you can plot from memory: $I_D=I_{DSS}$ at $V_{GS}=0$, $I_D=I_{DSS}/4$ at $V_{GS}=-V_P/2$, and $I_D=0$ at $V_{GS}=-V_P=-V_{GS(off)}$. It applies **only in the constant-current region**; in the ohmic region the same $V_{GS}$ gives a smaller current that depends on $V_{DS}$. Notice also that the curve is not a straight line, which is exactly why the transconductance changes with bias: $g_m=g_{m0}\left(1-\frac{|V_{GS}|}{V_P}\right)$ where $g_{m0}=2I_{DSS}/|V_P|$ is the transconductance at $V_{GS}=0$. Eliminating the gate voltage gives the form that is fastest in an exam, $g_m=\frac{2\sqrt{I_{DSS}I_D}}{|V_P|}$, and its companion $g_m=g_{m0}\sqrt{I_D/I_{DSS}}$. Maximum $g_m$ occurs at $V_{GS}=0$; $g_m$ falls to zero at pinch-off, so an amplifier biased near cutoff has almost no gain.

**Small-signal model and the limits of the simple gain formula.** For small signals the JFET is a voltage-controlled current source: a gate-source voltage $v_{gs}$ produces a drain current $g_m v_{gs}$, in parallel with the drain resistance $r_d=\Delta V_{DS}/\Delta I_D$ at constant $V_{GS}$, and the amplification factor is $\mu=g_m r_d$. With a drain resistor $R_D$ the voltage gain is $A_v=-g_m(R_D\parallel r_d)$, and the textbook shortcut $A_v=-g_mR_D$ is only valid when $r_d\gg R_D$. Because $r_d$ is typically tens to hundreds of kilohms, a $2.2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ drain resistor makes the shortcut good to a few percent, but a $47\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ load makes it badly optimistic. Three further limits matter: the gate-source junction must never be forward biased (about $+0.7\ \mathrm{V}$ destroys the high input resistance and can damage the device), the maximum drain current is bounded by $I_{DSS}$ so the square law fails if the bias asks for more, and the transconductance falls with temperature while $I_{DSS}$ also falls, which is why JFET bias is reasonably but not perfectly stable.

formulas.n: n-channel, constant-current region only. V_P is the pinch-off magnitude (a positive number) and V_GS is between 0 and -V_P. At V_GS = 0, I_D = I_DSS; at |V_GS| = V_P, I_D = 0.

formulas.q: Shockley law with a signed pinch-off voltage
formulas.n: Equivalent to the magnitude form ONLY if V_GS(off) is entered as the negative number. Substituting a positive V_P here gives (1 - (-2)/4)^2 = 2.25 and an impossible I_D above I_DSS.

formulas.q: Inverse Shockley: gate voltage for a target current
formulas.n: Take the square root before subtracting; the common error is to use the linear ratio I_D/I_DSS and get a gate voltage that is far too small.

formulas.q: Pinch-off boundary in the output characteristic
formulas.n: For V_DS below this the device is in the ohmic region and Shockley does not apply. Example: V_GS = -2 V, V_P = 4 V requires V_DS >= 2 V for constant current.
The largest g_m the device can give, in siemens (A/V). Compare with the data sheet g_fs at the intended bias point, which is always smaller.
Use the first form when V_GS is known and the second when I_D is known. g_m falls linearly with V_GS but only as the square root of I_D.
Quick bias check: at I_D = I_DSS/4 the transconductance is halved. Using the linear ratio I_D/I_DSS instead of the square root overestimates g_m by 2x in that example.

formulas.q: Voltage gain of the common-source stage
formulas.n: The simple form assumes r_d >> R_D. The negative sign is the 180 degree phase inversion of the common-source connection.

formulas.e: r_d = \frac{\Delta V_{DS}}{\Delta I_D} \ \mathrm{at\ constant\ } V_{GS}, \qquad \mu = g_m r_d
formulas.n: r_d comes from the slope of the output curves; a flatter curve means a larger r_d. mu is dimensionless. For r_d = 83 kohm and g_m = 3 mS, mu = 250.
Rough small-signal on-resistance with the gate shorted to the source and a small V_DS. It rises steeply as V_GS approaches V_GS(off).

problems.prompt: An n-channel JFET has $I_{DSS}=12\ \mathrm{mA}$ and $V_P=4\ \mathrm{V}$ (so $V_{GS(off)}=-4\ \mathrm{V}$). Find $I_D$ for $V_{GS}=-1\ \mathrm{V}$ and for $V_{GS}=-3\ \mathrm{V}$, and state the minimum $V_{DS}$ needed for each answer to be valid.
steps: Validity for case a: V_DS >= V_GS + V_P = -1 + 4 = 3 V
Validity for case b: V_DS >= -3 + 4 = 1 V
Sanity check with the memorised points: I_D = I_DSS = 12 mA at V_GS = 0, I_D = I_DSS/4 = 3 mA at V_GS = -2 V, and I_D = 0 at V_GS = -4 V
problems.ans: I_D = 6.75 mA at V_GS = -1 V (needs V_DS >= 3 V) and I_D = 0.75 mA at V_GS = -3 V (needs V_DS >= 1 V).
problems.trap: Interpolating linearly between the memorised points. Halfway from 0 to -4 V is -2 V, and the linear guess of 6 mA is wrong: the square law gives exactly 3 mA there, and -1 V gives 6.75 mA rather than 9 mA. The transfer curve is a parabola, not a line.

steps: Read straight off the table: **6.75** mA at −1 V and **0.75** mA at −3 V.
Boundary from the same row: `X+4` → **3** V at −1 V and **1** V at −3 V.
calc.note: The table exposes the parabola: −2 V gives exactly 3 mA, not the 6 mA a linear guess predicts.

problems.prompt: The same JFET ($I_{DSS}=12\ \mathrm{mA}$, $V_P=4\ \mathrm{V}$) must be biased at $I_D=8\ \mathrm{mA}$. Find the required $V_{GS}$ and the resulting $V_{DS(sat)}$.
steps: Boundary: V_DS(sat) = V_GS + V_P = -0.734 + 4 = 3.27 V, so the drain supply must allow at least 3.27 V across the device
problems.trap: Using the linear ratio: |V_GS| = 4(1 - 8/12) = 1.33 V. That looks plausible and is nearly twice the correct answer; the square root is required because the Shockley equation is quadratic in V_GS.

calc.note: The linear ratio gives 1.33 V, nearly double, because Shockley is quadratic in $V_{GS}$.

problems.prompt: For the same device biased at $V_{GS}=-2\ \mathrm{V}$ (so $I_D=3\ \mathrm{mA}$), find $g_{m0}$ and $g_m$ two ways.
steps: Second route: g_m = 2*sqrt(I_DSS*I_D)/|V_P| = 2*sqrt(12 mA * 3 mA)/4 V
sqrt(36e-6 A^2) = 6 mA, so g_m = 2(6 mA)/4 V = 3 mS, which matches
problems.ans: g_m0 = 6 mS at V_GS = 0 and g_m = 3 mS at the V_GS = -2 V bias point.
problems.trap: Reporting g_m = g_m0 = 6 mS at every bias point. The transconductance is halved at |V_GS| = V_P/2 and falls to zero at pinch-off, so quoting the data-sheet maximum g_fs for a device biased near cutoff doubles the predicted gain.

calc.note: $g_m = g_{m0}$ only at $V_{GS} = 0$; quoting the data-sheet $g_{fs}$ doubles the gain.

problems.prompt: The stage uses $R_D=2.2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ and the bias of the previous problem ($g_m=3\ \mathrm{mS}$, $r_d=83\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$). Find the voltage gain both with and without $r_d$, in ratio and in dB.
steps: In dB: 20*log10(6.43) = 16.2 dB, against 20*log10(6.6) = 16.4 dB for the shortcut, an error of only 0.2 dB
problems.ans: A_v = -6.6 by the shortcut and -6.43 exactly, i.e. 16.2 dB with 180 degree phase inversion.
problems.trap: Assuming the shortcut is always safe. Here R_D is only 2.6 percent of r_d so the error is small, but with R_D = 47 kohm the exact gain is -g_m(47k || 83k) = -3 mS * 30.0 kohm = -90 instead of -141, a 3.9 dB error that would ruin a gain budget.

steps: `20log(6.43)` → **16.2** dB against **16.4** dB for the shortcut, only 0.2 dB here.
calc.note: With $R_D = 47$ k$\Omega$ the shortcut is 3.9 dB optimistic; check $r_d$ against $R_D$ first.

problems.prompt: At $V_{GS}=-2\ \mathrm{V}$ the drain current is $3.00\ \mathrm{mA}$ at $V_{DS}=10\ \mathrm{V}$ and $3.12\ \mathrm{mA}$ at $V_{DS}=20\ \mathrm{V}$. Find $r_d$ and the amplification factor $\mu$. Then estimate the change in $I_D$ for a $50\ \mathrm{mV}$ step in $V_{GS}$ and compare with the exact Shockley value.
steps: r_d = delta_V_DS/delta_I_D = (20 - 10) V / (3.12 - 3.00) mA = 10 V / 0.12 mA = 83.3 kohm
Small-signal estimate: delta_I_D = g_m*delta_V_GS = (3 mS)(50 mV) = 0.15 mA
Exact at V_GS = -1.95 V: I_D = 12 mA*(1 - 1.95/4)^2 = 12 mA*(0.5125)^2 = 3.152 mA, so the true step is 0.152 mA
problems.ans: r_d = 83.3 kohm, mu = 250, and delta_I_D = 0.15 mA by g_m against 0.152 mA exactly (about 1 percent low).
problems.trap: Computing r_d as V_DS/I_D = 10/3.00 mA = 3.33 kohm. Drain resistance is a slope, delta_V_DS over delta_I_D, not a DC operating-point ratio. A related error is calling mu dimensionless current gain when it is the voltage amplification factor g_m*r_d.

calc.note: $V_{DS}/I_D$ would give 3.33 k$\Omega$, 25x wrong; $r_d$ is $\Delta V_{DS}/\Delta I_D$.

traps: **Mixing the sign conventions for $V_P$ and $V_{GS}$.** Entering $V_P=+4\ \mathrm{V}$ in $I_D=I_{DSS}(1-V_{GS}/V_P)^2$ with $V_{GS}=-2\ \mathrm{V}$ gives $(1.5)^2=2.25$ and $I_D=27\ \mathrm{mA}$, four and a half times $I_{DSS}$ and physically impossible. Use the magnitude form $\left(1-|V_{GS}|/V_P\right)^2$ or carry $V_{GS(off)}=-V_P$ with its sign.

**Applying the Shockley equation in the ohmic region.** It is valid only for $V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{GS(off)}$. Below that boundary the channel is not pinched off and the current depends on $V_{DS}$, so using the square law there overstates the current.

**Thinking $I_{DSS}$ is the absolute maximum drain current.** $I_{DSS}$ is defined at $V_{GS}=0$ and $V_{DS}\ge|V_P|$, and it is also the largest current the square law can produce. Any calculation returning $I_D>I_{DSS}$ means a sign or convention error.

**Treating $g_m$ as proportional to $I_D$.** It goes as $\sqrt{I_D}$, so halving the drain current reduces $g_m$ by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$, not 2. Quoting the data-sheet $g_{fs}$ maximum for a bias point near cutoff is the same error in disguise.

**Assuming the gate draws a little current or needs a bias supply.** The gate junction is reverse biased, so $I_G$ is nanoamps and a gate resistor exists only to set the DC reference and the input impedance. A forward-biased gate (about $+0.7\ \mathrm{V}$) collapses the input resistance and can destroy the device.
**Ignoring $r_d$ in the gain.** $A_v=-g_mR_D$ is valid only while $r_d\gg R_D$; with a large drain resistor the exact $A_v=-g_m(R_D\parallel r_d)$ can be several dB lower.
